map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: By the time the bell rang, Ana has already written three pages of her story.
By the time the bell rang, Ana had already written three pages of her story.
By the time the bell rang, Ana has already wrote three pages of her story.
By the time the bell rang, Ana had already wrote three pages of her story.
correct_answer: By the time the bell rang, Ana had already written three pages of her story.
error_sites: present perfect "has" used instead of past perfect "had" for an action completed before a past time
simple past "wrote" used instead of the past participle "written" after had/has

student_error.By the time the bell rang, Ana has alrea: uses present perfect because 'already' sounds like it goes with 'has,' ignoring the past time 'rang'
uses the everyday spoken forms 'has' and 'wrote' without checking either against the rule
student_error.By the time the bell rang, Ana had alrea: uses the simple past 'wrote' after 'had' instead of the past participle

explanation: 'By the time the bell rang' sets a point in the past, and the writing was finished before it, so the past perfect 'had written' is needed. The perfect tenses use the past participle 'written,' not the simple past 'wrote.' Only the key has both.
varied_dimension: past perfect vs present perfect; past participle form

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Either Marcus or his older sisters is going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
Neither Marcus or his older sisters is going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
Neither Marcus or his older sisters are going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
Either Marcus or his older sisters are going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
correct_answer: Either Marcus or his older sisters are going to walk the dog after dinner tonight.
error_sites: "Neither" paired with "or" instead of "Either" (or "nor")
singular verb "is" used though the nearer subject "sisters" is plural

student_error.Either Marcus or his older sisters is go: makes the verb agree with the first subject, 'Marcus,' instead of the nearer subject, 'sisters'
student_error.Neither Marcus or his older sisters is g: pairs 'neither' with 'or' as in everyday speech and agrees the verb with 'Marcus'
student_error.Neither Marcus or his older sisters are: pairs 'neither' with 'or' as in everyday speech instead of 'either...or' or 'neither...nor'

explanation: Correlative conjunctions come in fixed pairs: 'either...or' and 'neither...nor.' 'Neither...or' mixes the pairs. When two subjects are joined by 'either...or,' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here the plural 'sisters,' so 'are' is correct. Only the key uses a matching pair and 'are.'
varied_dimension: correlative conjunction pair; verb agreement with the nearer of two subjects

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Ms. Patel asked Leila and I to hand out the tests, and later her and I collected them.
Ms. Patel asked Leila and me to hand out the tests, and later her and I collected them.
Ms. Patel asked Leila and me to hand out the tests, and later she and I collected them.
Ms. Patel asked Leila and I to hand out the tests, and later she and I collected them.
correct_answer: Ms. Patel asked Leila and me to hand out the tests, and later she and I collected them.
error_sites: subjective "I" used in the compound object of "asked"
objective "her" used in the compound subject of "collected"

student_error.Ms. Patel asked Leila and I to hand out: chooses each pronoun by how it sounds next to another name instead of by its job in the sentence
student_error.Ms. Patel asked Leila and me to hand out: uses 'her' in a compound subject because 'her and I' is common in speech
student_error.Ms. Patel asked Leila and I to hand out: believes 'and I' is always more correct than 'and me'

explanation: 'Leila and me' is the object of 'asked,' so the objective pronoun 'me' is correct (Ms. Patel asked me). 'She and I' is the subject of 'collected,' so the subjective pronoun 'she' is correct (she collected). Only the key uses the right case in both places.
varied_dimension: objective pronoun in a compound object; subjective pronoun in a compound subject

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: My brother and I built the birdhouse ourselves, but Dad cut all the wood hisself.
My brother and I built the birdhouse ourselves, but Dad cut all the wood himself.
My brother and myself built the birdhouse ourselves, but Dad cut all the wood himself.
My brother and myself built the birdhouse ourselves, but Dad cut all the wood hisself.
correct_answer: My brother and I built the birdhouse ourselves, but Dad cut all the wood himself.
error_sites: reflexive/intensive "myself" used as part of the subject instead of "I"
nonstandard intensive form "hisself" instead of "himself"

student_error.My brother and I built the birdhouse our: builds the intensive pronoun from 'his' by analogy with 'myself' and 'yourself'
student_error.My brother and myself built the birdhous: uses 'myself' as a subject because it sounds more formal than 'I'
treats -self pronouns as ordinary pronouns that can go anywhere and forms them from the possessive

explanation: An intensive pronoun emphasizes a noun already in the sentence; it cannot serve as the subject, so 'My brother and I' is correct, not 'My brother and myself.' The standard intensive for 'Dad' is 'himself'; 'hisself' is not a standard form. Only the key uses both correctly.
varied_dimension: intensive pronoun misused as a subject; nonstandard intensive pronoun form

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Hikers who want to reach the top before dark should pack your bags the night before, so they can leave at sunrise.
Hikers who want to reach the top before dark should pack your bags the night before, so you can leave at sunrise.
Hikers who want to reach the top before dark should pack their bags the night before, so you can leave at sunrise.
Hikers who want to reach the top before dark should pack their bags the night before, so they can leave at sunrise.
correct_answer: Hikers who want to reach the top before dark should pack their bags the night before, so they can leave at sunrise.
error_sites: second-person "your" shifts away from the third-person antecedent "Hikers"
second-person "you" shifts away from the third-person antecedent "Hikers" in the later clause

student_error.Hikers who want to reach the top before: slips into giving advice to the reader ('pack your bags') in the middle of a sentence about hikers
switches from writing about hikers to talking to 'you' and stays there for the rest of the sentence
loses track of the antecedent 'Hikers' by the second clause and switches to 'you'

explanation: The antecedent 'Hikers' is third-person plural, so every pronoun referring to it must be third-person plural: 'their bags' and 'they can leave.' Changing to 'your' or 'you' is an inappropriate shift in pronoun person. Only the key stays consistent.
varied_dimension: shift in pronoun person in a possessive; shift in pronoun person in a subject

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Reaching for the top shelf, Grace knocked the jar of honey onto the floor that Mom had just bought.
Reaching for the top shelf, Grace's elbow knocked the jar of honey that Mom had just bought onto the floor.
Reaching for the top shelf, Grace knocked the jar of honey that Mom had just bought onto the floor.
Reaching for the top shelf, Grace's elbow knocked the jar of honey onto the floor that Mom had just bought.
correct_answer: Reaching for the top shelf, Grace knocked the jar of honey that Mom had just bought onto the floor.
error_sites: subject "Grace's elbow" leaves the opening participial phrase dangling (an elbow does not reach for a shelf)
relative clause "that Mom had just bought" misplaced after "the floor" instead of after "the jar of honey"

student_error.Reaching for the top shelf, Grace knocke: adds the extra detail at the end of the sentence without checking which noun it now describes
student_error.Reaching for the top shelf, Grace's elbo: names the body part that did the knocking without noticing the opening phrase must describe the subject
reads the sentence for meaning and does not check what either modifier is attached to

explanation: An opening participial phrase describes the subject that follows it. 'Grace' was reaching for the shelf, so 'Grace' must be the subject; 'Grace's elbow' makes the elbow do the reaching. A modifying clause belongs next to the noun it describes: Mom bought the jar of honey, not the floor. Only the key has both modifiers attached correctly.
varied_dimension: dangling participial phrase; misplaced relative clause

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Collecting old coins and stamps are a hobby that keeps my grandparents busy all winter.
Collecting old coins and stamps is a hobby that keep my grandparents busy all winter.
Collecting old coins and stamps are a hobby that keep my grandparents busy all winter.
Collecting old coins and stamps is a hobby that keeps my grandparents busy all winter.
correct_answer: Collecting old coins and stamps is a hobby that keeps my grandparents busy all winter.
error_sites: plural verb "are" used with the singular gerund-phrase subject "Collecting old coins and stamps"
plural verb "keep" in the relative clause whose antecedent is the singular "hobby"

student_error.Collecting old coins and stamps are a ho: makes the verb agree with the nearby plural 'coins and stamps' instead of the whole gerund phrase
student_error.Collecting old coins and stamps is a hob: makes the relative-clause verb agree with 'grandparents,' the plural noun after it, instead of 'hobby'
student_error.Collecting old coins and stamps are a ho: matches each verb to the closest plural noun instead of finding its real subject

explanation: The subject is the gerund phrase 'Collecting old coins and stamps,' which names one activity, so it takes the singular verb 'is.' In the relative clause, 'that' refers to 'a hobby,' which is singular, so the verb is 'keeps.' Only the key has both singular verbs.
varied_dimension: verb agreement with a gerund-phrase subject; verb agreement inside a relative clause

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Although the power went out during the storm, we played board games by candlelight, and nobody missed the TV.
The power went out during the storm, we played board games by candlelight, and nobody missed the TV.
The power went out during the storm, we played board games by candlelight, nobody missed the TV.
Although the power went out during the storm, we played board games by candlelight, nobody missed the TV.
correct_answer: Although the power went out during the storm, we played board games by candlelight, and nobody missed the TV.
error_sites: subordinating conjunction "Although" missing, leaving two independent clauses joined only by a comma ("Although the" vs "The")
coordinating conjunction "and" missing before the last independent clause

student_error.The power went out during the storm, we: writes the first idea as its own clause and joins it with a comma, not seeing that it needs a subordinating word
strings complete clauses together with commas, the way events are listed in speech
student_error.Although the power went out during the s: drops the joining word before the last clause because the comma seems to be enough

explanation: This is a compound-complex sentence. 'Although' makes the first clause dependent, so it can attach to the main clause with a comma. The last two clauses are both independent, so they must be joined by a comma plus a coordinating conjunction ('and'). Removing either word leaves independent clauses joined by a comma alone. Only the key is a correctly built sentence.
varied_dimension: subordinating conjunction that makes a clause dependent; coordinating conjunction joining independent clauses

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was used to wake up before sunrise.
Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was use to wake up before sunrise.
Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was used to waking up before sunrise.
Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was use to waking up before sunrise.
correct_answer: Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was used to waking up before sunrise.
error_sites: base form "use" written for the participle "used" in "was used to"
base verb "wake" used instead of the gerund "waking" after "was used to"

student_error.Having grown up on a farm, Mateo was use: confuses 'was used to' (accustomed to, followed by a gerund) with 'used to' (habit, followed by a base verb)
writes the phrase the way it sounds ('yoosta'), dropping the d of 'used' and treating 'to' as part of an infinitive
drops the d of 'used' because it is not heard before 'to'

explanation: In 'was used to' (meaning 'was accustomed to'), 'used' is a past participle and keeps its -d even though it is not heard before 'to.' The 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by a gerund: 'waking up.' Only the key uses both verbal forms correctly.
varied_dimension: past participle 'used' (not 'use') in 'be used to'; gerund after 'be used to'

map_area: Language: Understand, Edit for Grammar, Usage
choices: Read the directions, each question should be answered, and check your work before time runs out.
Read the directions, answer each question, and check your work before time runs out.
Read the directions, answer each question, and your work should be checked before time runs out.
Read the directions, each question should be answered, and your work should be checked before time runs out.
correct_answer: Read the directions, answer each question, and check your work before time runs out.
error_sites: shift from active imperative to passive voice in the second instruction ("each question should be answered" for "answer each question")
shift from active imperative to passive voice in the third instruction ("your work should be checked" for "check your work")

student_error.Read the directions, each question shoul: varies the middle instruction to avoid repeating the same pattern, switching it into the passive
student_error.Read the directions, answer each questio: turns the last instruction into a passive statement to sound more formal, shifting out of the active imperative
student_error.Read the directions, each question shoul: hears the last two parts as matching each other and does not notice that both have shifted away from the active command 'Read'

explanation: The sentence is a series of commands, so every item should be an active imperative verb: 'Read,' 'answer,' 'check.' 'Each question should be answered' and 'your work should be checked' shift into the passive voice and out of the imperative mood. Only the key keeps voice and mood consistent.
varied_dimension: shift from active imperative to passive voice in a middle item of a series; the same shift in the final item
